headline: Chatkal survey adit passes 800 of 1,500 metres; no contract, cost or financing yet
dek: Iradenergo's crews will keep digging through the winter, but the company calls the river cascade "a study, not a decision" and the upper sites still need clan consent.
paragraphs: Survey crews working for Iradenergo have dug about 800 metres of a planned 1,500-metre exploratory tunnel into the right bank of the Chatkal river at the valley mouth in Sary-Bulak District, the company said this week. Work in the adit will continue through the winter. The company still has no construction contract, cost estimate or financing to announce for the power stations it is meant to serve.

The adit follows the line a headrace tunnel would take for the first station of the Chatkal river cascade, which engineers put at roughly 30 MW. The site is on the ISEZ side of the line, close to the foothill villages of Uuk-Bulak and Tash-Bulak. The tunnel's purpose is narrow: to show what the rock is like along the route before anyone commits to a design. IradOne reported the figures on Monday.

Asked what the work amounts to, Iradenergo spokesman Vladislav Ten said the company has "no contract, cost or financing to announce". The cascade, he said, remains "a study, not a decision". Mr Ten did not give the number of people working underground or the survey budget, and said the findings would go into the feasibility study that is still being prepared.

The 30 MW figure is about a fifth of the roughly 146 MW that Iradenergo has said it is studying for the whole cascade, which Sary-Bulak district head Taalaibek Imashev first described to a residents' meeting in Sary-Bulak at the end of October. It is also about two per cent of the 1,440 MW at Toktogul, which supplies the export contracts and the winter peak. Iradenergo would buy the output of any Chatkal stations itself.

Mr Imashev welcomed the survey jobs for local crews. "Wages paid in the valley stay in the valley, and in winter there is little else on offer," he said. The Herald asked how many local people have been taken on; the district administration had not replied by deadline.

In Tash-Bulak, herder Mamat Sooronbai uulu said the tunnel mouth is not on the route his animals take, but the trucks are. "We were told it is only a survey. A survey does not need so many lorries," he said. Nobody has told the village what happens to the river road if building starts, he added.

Dr Bermet Asylova, a hydrologist at Talas State University, said a rock survey answers only half the question. Tunnelling data tell engineers whether a headrace can be driven and lined at a sensible price, she said, but the economics of small run-of-river stations depend on winter flow, and a station that produces little in January is a poor partner for a grid that peaks in the cold months. She said she had seen no published flow record for the Chatkal that she could cite.

The larger obstacle lies upstream. The upper sites are in the Chatkal Highlands, where the river and its catchment are held by the Naiman and Sarybagysh clans, and no stretch of the cascade there can be built without the clan councils' agreement. Iradenergo has said nothing in public about talks with them. A request for comment sent to the Kurultai Chancellery had not been answered by deadline.

What happens next depends on the study. Iradenergo has set no date for its completion. Under the company's own wording, a decision on whether to build would come only after it, and any contract or financing would then have to be published. Until then, the tally is 800 metres dug, 700 to go, and nothing else announced.

iradone.headline: Chatkal Survey Tunnel Passes 800 Metres; Iradenergo Calls Cascade "a Study"
